situation: A chain of 25 frozen-yogurt shops saw profit fall from $3M to $1.8M in a year, while revenue held steady.
reason_to_start_there: Revenue is flat, so the drop is in costs, and ingredients are the biggest cost in a self-serve shop
specific_request_examples: Ingredient cost per cup by month for two years; labor hours per store by month
model_answer: With revenue flat, the drop is likely in costs, but I'd confirm price and mix too. I'd split profit into price per cup, ingredients per cup, labor, and rent. I'd start with ingredient cost per cup by month for two years, since ingredients are the biggest cost.

situation: An online pet-supply store's average delivery time rose from 2 days to 5 this quarter.
reason_to_start_there: It splits our own delay from the carrier's, and it's the part we control
specific_request_examples: Days from order to dispatch by week, this quarter against last; carrier transit days by region
model_answer: I'd split delivery time into order-to-dispatch days, carrier transit, stock-outs, and order volume against capacity. I'd start with order-to-dispatch days by week, this quarter against last, since that's the part we control and shows whether the delay is ours.

situation: A US frozen-burrito brand wants to know whether it could reach £20M of yearly sales in the UK within four years.
reason_to_start_there: £20M only works if the category is several times larger; if it's small, nothing else matters
specific_request_examples: UK frozen Mexican-food sales by year for five years; supermarket listing fees per store
vague_request_examples: Information on the UK market; competitor data
model_answer: I'd split it into the UK market's size and growth, competitors' shares, getting into supermarkets, and margin after import costs. I'd start with UK frozen Mexican-food sales by year for five years, since £20M is only realistic if the category is several times bigger.

situation: Running costs for a city's 400 police cars rose 20% in three years, while the fleet's average age rose from 3 to 6 years.
reason_to_start_there: The fleet doubled in age, and older cars cost more to fix
specific_request_examples: Repair cost per car per year by car age, for three years; fuel cost per mile by year
model_answer: I'd split running costs per car into maintenance and repairs, fuel, insurance, and miles driven. I'd start with repair cost per car by car age over three years, since the fleet's average age doubled and older cars cost more to fix.

situation: A wedding venue is booked every Saturday two years ahead but is half-empty on Fridays and Sundays. It is setting next year's prices.
best_starting_point: Demand by day of the week
reason_to_start_there: Saturday demand far exceeds supply while other days have room, so prices should differ by day
specific_request_examples: Booking lead time and inquiries turned away by day of the week for two years; competitor venues' prices by day
model_answer: Prices turn on demand by day, couples' budgets, competitor venues' prices, and our cost per event. I'd start with inquiries turned away and booking lead time by day of the week for two years, since Saturdays are oversold while Fridays and Sundays have room.

situation: A craft-supply website wants to double revenue in three years. Today 80% of its sales come from repeat customers.
reason_to_start_there: Doubling needs many more buyers, and only a fifth of sales come from new ones, so acquisition looks weak
specific_request_examples: First-time visitors and their conversion rate by month for two years; repeat orders per customer per year
model_answer: I'd split revenue into new customers, repeat purchases, order value, and new product ranges. I'd start with first-time visitors and their conversion rate by month for two years, since only a fifth of sales come from new customers, so winning new buyers is likely the gap.

situation: A city's building-permit approvals now take 14 weeks on average, up from 6.
reason_to_start_there: Splitting the 14 weeks by step shows where the extra time goes
specific_request_examples: Average weeks per review step for this year and last; share of applications sent back for corrections
model_answer: I'd split approval time into time in each review step, rounds of corrections, application volume, and reviewer capacity. I'd start with average weeks in each step this year against last, since that shows where the extra 8 weeks come from.

situation: A regional chain of 15 mattress stores lost 20% of its sales after online mattress brands began selling at 30% less.
reason_to_start_there: Knowing which products and price points lost sales shows whether the online brands are the cause and what to defend
specific_request_examples: Sales by price band and product this year against last; store visits and sales per visit by month
model_answer: I'd look at which products lost sales, the price gap with online brands, store traffic against conversion, and what stores offer that online can't. I'd start with sales by price band this year against last, to see whether the losses sit where online brands compete.

situation: A sports-drink brand's zero-sugar version launched six months ago, and sales are 40% below plan.
reason_to_start_there: Sales are stores carrying it times sales per store; if few stores stock it, nothing else matters
specific_request_examples: Stores carrying it against plan, by retailer; sales per store per week against plan
model_answer: I'd split sales into stores carrying it, shoppers trying it, repeat buying, and sales taken from the regular drink. I'd start with stores carrying it against plan by retailer, since sales are distribution times sales per store, and low distribution would explain most of the gap.

situation: A waste-hauling company wants to know whether a rival priced at $40M is worth buying.
reason_to_start_there: The rival's own cash flow is the base of its value; synergies come on top
specific_request_examples: The rival's profit by customer contract for three years; contract end dates and renewal rates
model_answer: I'd split it into the rival's own profit, savings from combining routes, its customer contracts, and price against value. I'd start with its profit by contract for three years, since its own cash flow is the base of what it's worth; route savings come on top.

situation: Lunch lines in a school cafeteria now take 25 minutes, up from 10.
best_starting_point: Time per student at each station (or the arrival pattern)
reason_to_start_there: The line is arrivals against serving speed: a slow station sets the pace, and a lunch-bell surge can overwhelm any station
specific_request_examples: Seconds per student at each station this term against last; students arriving per minute in the first 10 minutes
model_answer: The line depends on arrivals, time per student at each station, staff on the line, and payment. I'd start with seconds per student at each station this term against last, since the slowest station sets the pace, then students arriving per minute.

situation: A dairy farm is deciding whether to buy a $500,000 robotic milking system.
reason_to_start_there: Labor is the main cost the robot replaces, so it drives the payback
specific_request_examples: Hours spent milking per week and the wage per hour; milk yield per cow per day now
vague_request_examples: Farm costs; information on the robot
model_answer: I'd look at labor saved, any change in milk yield, the robot's full cost including upkeep and financing, and whether it can handle the herd. I'd start with hours spent milking per week and their cost, since labor is the main cost the robot replaces.

situation: A regional TV station's profit fell 40% in two years, while its viewership held steady.
reason_to_start_there: With viewers steady, falling revenue most likely comes from what advertisers pay as budgets move online
specific_request_examples: Average price per 30-second ad by daypart for three years; share of ad slots sold
model_answer: I'd split profit into ad prices, ad slots sold, fees from cable and streaming carriers, and programming costs. I'd start with average price per ad by daypart for three years, since viewers held steady, so advertisers paying less is the likeliest cause.

situation: A uniform-rental company serving businesses wants to grow revenue 25% in three years. It loses 15% of its accounts every year.
reason_to_start_there: Losing 15% a year means it must replace a big share of revenue before growing
specific_request_examples: Accounts lost per year by reason and industry; revenue per account for new and long-time accounts
model_answer: I'd split growth into accounts lost, new accounts won, revenue per account, and new services. I'd start with accounts lost per year by reason and industry, since losing 15% a year means most new sales just replace what leaves.

situation: A zoo is considering raising adult tickets from $25 to $30.
reason_to_start_there: The decision turns on how many visitors a $5 rise would lose
specific_request_examples: Attendance after past price changes, by visitor type; share of visits from members against day tickets
model_answer: I'd look at how visitors respond to price, the mix of members and day visitors, spending inside the zoo, and prices at nearby attractions. I'd start with attendance after past price changes by visitor type, since the decision turns on how many visitors $5 would lose.

situation: An online retailer's shipping cost per order rose 18% this year, after its main carrier began pricing by box size.
reason_to_start_there: The carrier's new pricing charges by box size, so oversized boxes are the likeliest cause
specific_request_examples: Share of orders by box size and fill rate this year against last; cost per order by shipping speed
model_answer: I'd split shipping cost per order into box size, carrier rates, shipping speed, and orders sent in more than one box. I'd start with orders by box size and how full the boxes are, this year against last, since the carrier now charges by box size.

situation: An appliance-repair company's technicians now complete 3.1 jobs a day, down from 4.0.
reason_to_start_there: A job that needs a second visit for parts takes two slots; longer drives between jobs are the other likely cause
specific_request_examples: Share of jobs needing a second visit, by appliance type, this year against last; travel minutes between jobs
model_answer: I'd split jobs per day into travel time, time per repair, repeat visits for parts, and gaps from cancellations. I'd start with the share of jobs needing a second visit, by appliance, this year against last, since a repeat visit takes a whole extra slot.

situation: A Brazilian electric-scooter maker wants to know whether to enter Mexico.
reason_to_start_there: Entry only makes sense if enough Mexicans would buy electric scooters
specific_request_examples: Electric-scooter sales in Mexico by year and city; average price paid
model_answer: Whether entry works depends on Mexican demand, competitors' prices, dealers to sell through, and import duties. I'd start with electric-scooter sales in Mexico by year and city, since entry only makes sense if demand is big and growing.

situation: A regional bank lost 10% of its deposits in a year after an online bank began paying 4% interest.
reason_to_start_there: Knowing which customers and balances left shows whether the online rate is the cause and who to defend
specific_request_examples: Deposits lost by customer segment and balance size this year; other products those customers held
model_answer: It depends on which deposits left, the rate gap, what else departing customers held with us, and the cost of matching. I'd start with deposits lost by customer segment and balance size over the past year, to see whether the losses sit where a 4% rate would bite.

situation: A spirits company's new canned cocktails sell well at first, but only 15% of buyers buy again, against 35% for rival brands.
reason_to_start_there: Trial is fine; the problem is repeat buying, so the reasons people don't rebuy come first
specific_request_examples: Survey of one-time buyers on why they didn't rebuy, by flavor; repeat rate by store type
model_answer: I'd look at product satisfaction, price against rivals, where and how it's displayed, and pack sizes. I'd start with a survey of one-time buyers on why they didn't buy again, by flavor, since trial is fine and repeat buying is where we trail rivals.

situation: A national health service's waiting list for hip replacements grew from 18 weeks to 30.
reason_to_start_there: The list grows when operations per week fall behind referrals, and capacity is the likelier constraint
specific_request_examples: Hip operations per week against referrals per week for two years; operations canceled for lack of beds
model_answer: I'd compare referrals with operations, and look at surgeon and theater capacity, bed shortages that block discharge, and cancellations. I'd start with operations per week against referrals per week for two years, to see whether capacity fell or demand rose.

situation: A national private-school group is deciding whether to buy 8 schools for $120M.
reason_to_start_there: Enrollment drives tuition revenue, so falling enrollment would undermine the value
specific_request_examples: Enrollment by school and grade for five years; tuition discounts as a share of list price
model_answer: I'd look at enrollment trends, tuition and discounts, teacher and building costs, and price against value. I'd start with enrollment by school and grade for five years, since enrollment drives revenue and a decline would undercut the $120M.

situation: A chain of 40 casual-dining restaurants has lost money for two years.
reason_to_start_there: Knowing whether losses are spread or concentrated decides between fixing the chain and closing sites
specific_request_examples: Profit by restaurant for two years; guests per restaurant per week
model_answer: I'd look at results by restaurant, guest traffic, average check, and food and labor costs. I'd start with profit by restaurant for two years, since if a few sites cause most of the losses, closing them may matter more than any chain-wide fix.

situation: An investor asks whether the US pet-cremation industry is attractive.
reason_to_start_there: An industry is only attractive if demand is large and growing
specific_request_examples: Pet deaths per year and the share cremated, for five years; average price per cremation
model_answer: I'd look at demand, how fragmented the industry is, prices and margins, and how business arrives through vets. I'd start with pet deaths per year and the share cremated over five years, since attractiveness starts with large, growing demand.

situation: A grain farm is deciding whether to build a $2M grain-drying and storage facility.
reason_to_start_there: Storage pays mainly by letting the farm sell after harvest, when prices are usually higher
specific_request_examples: Monthly grain prices for five years, harvest against spring; current drying costs per bushel
model_answer: I'd look at the price gain from selling after harvest, drying-cost savings, the facility's building and running costs, and crop volume. I'd start with monthly grain prices for five years, harvest against spring, since storage pays mainly by letting us sell later at higher prices.

situation: An online-courses company's profit fell this year even though revenue grew 20%. Its marketing spend doubled over the same year.
reason_to_start_there: Growth bought with marketing can cost more than it brings in
specific_request_examples: Marketing spend per new student by channel for two years; instructor payouts as a share of revenue
model_answer: I'd look at the cost to win each student, content production, instructor payouts, and platform costs. I'd start with marketing spend per new student by channel for two years, since growth bought with marketing can cost more than it brings in.

situation: A university IT help desk now takes 4 days to close a ticket, up from 1. Ticket volume and help-desk staffing are unchanged.
reason_to_start_there: Tickets usually wait in queues between teams, so handoffs explain most delays
specific_request_examples: Hours tickets wait in each queue, by ticket type, this term against last; share of tickets passed to another team
model_answer: I'd look at ticket volume, staff capacity, the mix of ticket types, and handoffs between teams. I'd start with hours tickets wait in each queue this term against last, since tickets usually sit between teams rather than with the person fixing them.

situation: A regional airport wants to grow passenger numbers 30%.
reason_to_start_there: Passengers come from the flights airlines choose to run, so the airport grows by winning routes
specific_request_examples: Routes flown from the airport and seats per week for three years; passengers in the area who drive to a larger airport
model_answer: I'd look at airlines and routes, local passengers who use a bigger airport, landing fees and incentives, and road and rail access. I'd start with routes and seats per week for three years, since passengers come from the flights airlines choose to run here.

situation: A country's electricity grid had twice as many outage minutes this year as five years ago.
reason_to_start_there: Splitting outage minutes by cause shows whether weather, equipment or demand drives the rise
specific_request_examples: Outage minutes by cause and region for five years; share of equipment past its design life
model_answer: I'd look at outage causes, equipment age, maintenance spending, and peak demand. I'd start with outage minutes by cause and region for five years, since that shows whether storms, aging equipment or peak load drives the doubling.

situation: A national car-dealer group is deciding whether to buy an online used-car platform.
reason_to_start_there: Many online car sellers lose money on each car; the deal only works if each sale can make money
specific_request_examples: Gross profit per car sold, by quarter for two years; reconditioning and delivery cost per car
model_answer: I'd look at the platform's profit per car, its growth, savings from sharing our inventory and financing, and the price against value. I'd start with gross profit per car by quarter for two years, since the deal only works if each sale can make money.

situation: A container-shipping line went from a $2B profit to a $300M loss in a year.
reason_to_start_there: A swing that large usually comes from freight rates, which can fall by half in a year
specific_request_examples: Average rate per container by trade lane by quarter for two years; volume carried by lane
model_answer: I'd split it into freight rates, volume carried, fuel costs, and ship charter costs. I'd start with average rate per container by trade lane by quarter, since a $2.3B swing usually comes from rates, which can halve in a year.

situation: A pension fund asks whether the US cell-tower industry is attractive for a 20-year investment.
reason_to_start_there: Tower income depends on carriers renting space, so their spending drives the industry
specific_request_examples: Carrier spending on tower leases by year for five years; average lease length and yearly price increases
model_answer: I'd look at carrier demand for tower space, lease terms, competition among tower owners, and the risk that satellites replace towers. I'd start with carrier spending on tower leases for five years, since tower income depends on carriers renting space.

situation: A startup needs to estimate how many home electric-car chargers are installed in the US each year.
best_starting_point: Share of EV buyers who install a charger
reason_to_start_there: It turns EV sales into chargers and varies most with housing
specific_request_examples: Share of EV buyers installing a home charger, by housing type; EV sales by year
model_answer: Chargers installed are EV sales times the share of EV buyers who install a charger, plus replacements. I'd start with the share of EV buyers who install a charger, by housing type for two years, since it varies most.

situation: A coastal city is deciding whether to build a $300M desalination plant.
best_starting_point: Cost of other water sources (or demand growth)
reason_to_start_there: The plant is worth it only if cheaper sources can't meet demand, and only if demand will outgrow current supply
specific_request_examples: Cost per cubic meter of desalination against conservation, reuse and imported water; water demand forecasts by year
model_answer: The decision turns on demand growth, the cost of other sources, the plant's cost, and the price of the power it would run on. I'd start with cost per cubic meter by water source (desalination, conservation, reuse, imports) over the next 20 years, since cheaper sources may meet demand.

situation: A drug company's best-selling drug faces its first generic competitor in 12 months.
reason_to_start_there: The response depends on how fast prices and share fall once generics arrive
specific_request_examples: Share and price lost by similar drugs in the first year after generics; revenue by payer type
model_answer: The response depends on revenue at risk, launching our own generic, pipeline drugs, and doctor and insurer loyalty. I'd start with market share and price lost by similar drugs in each quarter of their first year after generics, since that shows how fast revenue falls.

situation: A European ski-equipment maker has lost money for three seasons as snow seasons have shortened.
reason_to_start_there: Knowing where sales fell shows whether the problem is shorter seasons everywhere or a few products and countries
specific_request_examples: Sales by product line and country for five seasons; inventory and discounts at season end
model_answer: I'd look at sales by product and market, leftover inventory and discounting, factory costs, and products for other seasons. I'd start with sales by product line and country for five seasons, to see whether losses are everywhere or in a few products and markets.

situation: A national postal service with 4,000 branches wants non-mail revenue to reach 40% of its total.
reason_to_start_there: Parcels are growing fastest with online shopping, so they are the likeliest route to 40%
specific_request_examples: Parcel and returns volume and revenue by year for five years; branch visits by purpose
model_answer: I'd look at parcels and returns, services branches could add like banking and ID checks, branch traffic, and partnerships. I'd start with parcel and returns revenue by year for five years, since parcels grow fastest with online shopping and are the likeliest route to 40%.

situation: An offshore wind farm's turbines are available 88% of the time, against a 97% target.
reason_to_start_there: Downtime starts with what breaks, so failures by component show where to act
specific_request_examples: Downtime hours by component for two years; days waiting for a vessel or weather window per repair
model_answer: I'd split downtime into what fails, how long repairs take, waiting for vessels or weather, spare parts, and maintenance planning. I'd start with downtime hours by component for two years, since knowing what breaks most shows where to act.

situation: A European rail operator is setting prices for a new high-speed route that competes with budget airlines.
reason_to_start_there: Travelers compare door-to-door time and price with flights, so the airline offer sets the price range
specific_request_examples: Budget airline fares by day and time on the route; door-to-door travel times by rail and air
model_answer: I'd look at competing airline fares and trip times, what business and leisure travelers will pay, train capacity and expected load, and costs. I'd start with airline fares by day and time and door-to-door times, since travelers compare both with flying.

situation: A health insurer's administrative cost per member is 30% higher than its peers'.
reason_to_start_there: Claims handling is usually the largest admin cost, and manual processing is the common gap with peers
specific_request_examples: Cost per claim and share of claims handled automatically, against peers; calls per member per year
model_answer: I'd split admin cost into claims processing, customer-service calls per member, IT systems, and sales commissions. I'd start with cost per claim and the share handled automatically over two years, against peers, since claims are usually the biggest admin cost and manual handling the usual gap.
